title: Queen against rook III: breaking the third-rank defence
summary: The rook's barrier on the third and fourth ranks, the quiet move that breaks it, and the stalemate traps.
part.third.title: The third-rank barrier
part.third.summary: The rook blocks our king's path. A quiet queen move leaves it without a square.
part.best.title: The best defence
part.best.summary: Every rook escape falls, and against the best defence the queen switches sides until the diagonal position.
part.thirdA.title: The rook at the end, and the fourth rank
part.thirdA.summary: The king walks around and drives the rook away; the fourth-rank barrier falls the same way.
part.ponziani.title: The stalemate draws
part.ponziani.summary: A queen glued to a cornered king lets the rook offer itself with check. That is how Morozevich let it slip.
part.map.title: The map of the ending
part.map.summary: Every stage, from far away to Philidor, and the whole ending against the machine.
step.t_third: The rook, on the black king's third rank, blocks our king's path, and checks do not help. Think: which queen move leaves the rook without a safe square on its rank?
step.t_third.hint1: Count the squares on the rook's rank that each of our pieces guards. From somewhere else the queen would guard more, even if it looks like a retreat.
step.intro: This is the most stubborn defence in the endgame. The black king is on the edge and the rook, on its third rank, closes the way: our king cannot cross the marked line. As long as the rook has a safe square on that rank, there is no progress. It was at this barrier that Walter Browne got stuck against the computer in 1978, and Nunn warns that it cannot be worked out over the board: you have to know it beforehand. You will.
step.seven: Look at what each of our pieces watches on the rook's rank. The king takes c6, d6 and e6. The queen takes e6, f6 and g6. That leaves squares for the rook, and it sits happily on b6. Checking does not help: the black king shuffles from side to side behind the rook. What breaks the defence is a quiet move, and it looks like a retreat.
step.quietMove: The queen has left the seventh rank and gone to f4. Now look at the rook's rank with Black to move. On c6, d6 and e6 the king takes. On f6 and h6 the queen takes. On a6 and g6 the rook falls to a fork in two checks. Off the rank it is worse: our king enters on c6 with a mating threat. The rook has no square, and the black king is forced to move. Let us see the forks first.
step.rg6: The rook went to g6. Two checks: the first on the back rank, the second attacks king and rook.
step.rg6.hint: Qf8+ and, when the king goes to d7, Qf7+. From f7 the diagonal reaches g6.
step.rg6.done: A fork. That is why g6 was not a safe square.
step.ra6: The rook went to a6, the other end. The same pattern on the other side: a back-rank check and a fork.
step.ra6.hint: Qb8+ and, after Ke7, Qb7+. From b7 the queen attacks a6.
step.ra6.done: Both ends of the rank fall the same way. The queen on f4 was looking at b8 and f8 at the same time.
step.rb7: The rook retreated to b7, giving up the rank. Now our king can cross. To which square?
step.rb7.hint: The square that attacks the rook and leaves the black king with no way out along the back rank.
step.rb7.done: The king has crossed the barrier, the rook is attacked and the queen threatens mate on f8. Black cannot hold both.
step.switch: Now the best defence: after Qf4 the black king goes to d7. The queen changes sides with checks, a4 and a7, and the rook is forced to interpose on b7. One more check on c5 and our king enters on d6.
step.switch.hint: Qf4, Qa4+, Qa7+, Qc5+ and Kd6. The queen crosses to the other side with tempo, and the rook leaves the third rank.
step.switch.done: The barrier has fallen: our king is on d6 and the rook has ended up on the second rank. From here on it is last lesson.
step.home: The rook went to g7 looking for checks. Put the queen on e5: the rook returns to c7 and the diagonal position appears. Then the triangle you know.
step.home.hint: Qe5 and, after Rc7, Qf4, Qf5+ and Qe5.
step.home.done: The diagonal position, with Black to move. The rook goes to b7, the king gives the discovered check on c6 and it is Philidor. From the third rank to there, about ten moves.
step.t_thirdA: The rook is still on the third rank, but now at its end. Think: do you really need a queen move, or can our king drive the rook away?
step.t_thirdA.hint1: A rook at the end of the rank can be attacked from below by the king, if it walks around.
step.a6: The second third-rank position you need to know: the rook at the end, on a6. Here the queen move is not needed. Our king walks round: c5 and then b5, attacking the rook from below. It has nowhere to run along the rank.
step.around: Go round with the king. Between the two king moves the queen goes to e7 and pushes the black king out of the way.
step.around.done: The rook has been driven off the third rank and only a7 is left: the second-rank defence, which you already know how to win.
step.fourth: One step earlier: the fourth rank. The black king is still two ranks from the edge and the rook cuts our king off on the line above. It is the easiest barrier to undo. The queen gives a check and goes to e6, taking squares from the black king; then our king walks round to attack the rook. Nunn prefers to go via d3: on d4 the rook would go to a1, on the same diagonal as our king, from where it threatens checks from two sides. The tablebase says both routes win in the same time; via d3 it is simpler.
step.fourthA: Undo the fourth rank. Check on f7, queen to e6, king via d3 and d4. When the rook runs to c1, the queen goes to e3 and, with the rook back on c6, check on e7 and king to d5.
step.fourthA.hint: Qf7+, Qe6, Kd3, Kd4, Qe3, Qe7+ and Kd5.
step.fourthA.done: Turn the board sideways: black king on the b-file, rook on the c-file, our king on d5. It is the third rank, and you know how to break it.
step.t_ponziani: Queen and king close, the black king cornered, and still this position is a draw. Think: what can the rook do, and which of our pieces is badly placed?
step.t_ponziani.hint1: Look at the rook's checks and count the black king's squares after each capture.
step.ponziani: Now the draws. This position is Ponziani's, from 1782, with Black to move. The rook checks on g7. If our king goes to f6, it checks on g6 and, if captured, the black king is stalemated. If the king goes to h6, it checks on h7 and so on for ever. The flaw in the position is the queen on e6, hugging the black king. With the queen at a distance this does not happen.
step.desperado: And this one is from 2006. Morozevich had the queen against Jakovenko and got here after more than a hundred moves. He has just brought the king closer, and Black plays the rook to f2 with check. If the king takes, stalemate. If the queen takes, stalemate. If the king runs, the rook keeps checking and offering itself. A draw. Queen and king hugging the cornered king: the same illness.
step.moro: Go back two moves and win the game Morozevich did not win. The queen goes far away, to the centre; then the king approaches without letting the rook sacrifice itself.
step.moro.hint: Qe5. After Kg1, Kg3; to the rook check, Kh3.
step.moro.done: The rook is attacked, has no useful check and cannot sacrifice itself: the queen, from afar, leaves the black king a square. Queen far, king near.
step.t_browne: One of the worst positions in the ending: our king is far from the black king and the rook is loose. Think: what is the plan, stage by stage, up to the Philidor position?
step.t_browne.hint1: Recall what you have learned, from the end back: Philidor, the second rank, the third. First, bring the king up without walking into checks.
step.map: The whole map, back to front. This is the position from Browne's rematch, one of the worst there is: with perfect play the rook falls in 31 moves. One: bring the king close and take the rook's checks away. Two: the fourth rank is undone by walking round with the king, and the ladder walks the black king down. Three: the third rank is broken with the quiet queen move. Four: the second rank, with a check and the king sideways. Five: Philidor, the triangle and the fork. You have fifty moves, and you know every stage.
step.recap: Three rules from this lesson. One: against the third rank with the rook near its king, the queen leaves the seventh for f4, and the rook has no square. Two: with the rook at the end of the rank, the king walks round and drives it off. Three: in the corner, queen far away; if the rook can offer itself with check, count the black king's squares before you move.
step.finish: Your turn against the machine, from the third-rank defence. Break the barrier, go through the second rank, reach Philidor and win the rook. It is the whole endgame, minus the beginning.
ex.e01: White to move. The third-rank defence. Which move leaves the rook without a safe square?
ex.e01.hint: It is not a check. The queen leaves the seventh rank and stays on the same file.
ex.e01.solution: Qf4. From the f-file the queen watches f6 and f8, and along the diagonals it reaches b8 and h6. Every rook move loses, and the black king has to come out from behind it. Qf3 and Qf2 also win, but without these forks.
ex.e02: White to move. The rook went to g6. Win it with two checks.
ex.e02.hint: First the back rank; then the square from which the diagonal reaches g6.
ex.e02.solution: Qf8+ and, after Kd7, Qf7+. A fork of king and rook.
ex.e03: White to move. The rook went to a6. Win it with two checks.
ex.e03.hint: The same pattern on the other side: the back rank and then the square diagonally next to the rook.
ex.e03.solution: Qb8+ and, after Ke7, Qb7+. From b7 the queen checks and attacks a6.
ex.e04: White to move. The rook dropped to b2. Which check wins it?
ex.e04.hint: A square on the black king's diagonal and on the long diagonal of b2.
ex.e04.solution: Qf6+. The queen checks d8 along one diagonal and attacks b2 along the other.
ex.e05: White to move. The black king stepped out to d7. Switch the queen to the other side with checks and get the rook off the third rank.
ex.e05.hint: Two checks along the a-file, and the rook has to interpose. Then a check on the c-file.
ex.e05.solution: Qa4+, Qa7+ and, after Rb7, Qc5+. The rook was forced to interpose on the second rank, and next move our king enters on d6.
ex.e06: White to move. Third rank with the rook at the end, on a6. How do you drive it off?
ex.e06.hint: The king does the work here, from below the rook. The queen only helps with one quiet move.
ex.e06.solution: Kc5 and, after Kc8, Qe7. The king goes on to b5 and attacks the rook, which has only a7: it has become the second rank.
ex.e07: White to move. The position from Morozevich against Jakovenko. Win without letting the rook sacrifice itself.
ex.e07.hint: The queen goes to the centre, far from the black king. Only then does the king approach, along the g-file.
ex.e07.solution: Qe5, and after Kg1, Kg3. To the check on g2 the king goes to h3 and the rook is lost. In the game, the check on g3 followed by Kf3 allowed the rook to f2 with check, and a draw by stalemate.
ex.e08: White to move. The rook is on the third rank and our king is far away. Place the queen and bring the king in front of the black king.
ex.e08.hint: The queen goes to the square it occupies in the lesson position. Then the king walks along the fifth rank, attacking the rook.
ex.e08.solution: Qf7, Ke5 and Kd5. With each king step the rook has to change square, and it ends up on b6 or a6: the two positions from the lesson.
ex.e09: White to move. The fourth-rank defence. Take squares from the black king with the queen and start walking round with the king.
ex.e09.hint: A check, a quiet queen move on the e-file, and the king steps back one square to go round.
ex.e09.solution: Qf7+, Qe6 and Kd3. The queen on e6 ties the black king to the edge, and the white king goes to attack the rook from the side. Via d4 it also wins, but the rook would have the square a1, on the king's diagonal.
ex.e10: White to move. After Qf4 the black king went to c8. Bring the king to b5 and drive the rook off the third rank.
ex.e10.hint: King to c5 first. The queen helps with a move on the e-file and a check on e7.
ex.e10.solution: Kc5, Qe4, Qe7+ and Kb5. The rook, attacked on a6, has only a7: the second-rank defence.
ex.e11: Black to move and draw. The white queen has come too close. Save the game with the rook.
ex.e11.hint: Check. And if the white king comes to f6, another check, on a square where the rook can be captured.
ex.e11.solution: Rg7+ and, after Kf6, Rg6+. If the king or the queen takes the rook, the black king is stalemated; if the king runs, the checks go on. It is Ponziani's draw, from 1782.
key.third: The third-rank defence with the rook on b6, from Nunn, as shown on Wikipedia. It is broken with Qf4.
key.thirdA: The third rank with the rook at the end, on a6: the king walks round via c5 and b5.
key.fourth: The fourth-rank defence, from Nunn, via Wikipedia: Qf7+, Qe6 and the king goes round via d3.
key.ponziani: Ponziani's draw (1782): with Black to move the rook checks on g7, g6 and h7, and capturing it is stalemate.
key.browne: The position from Browne's rematch against Belle (1978): with perfect play the rook falls in 31 moves.
history: In 1895 a whole book on this endgame alone came out in London, signed by one Euclid, and even so, for almost a century, the manuals treated queen against rook as a simple matter. Ken Thompson's database, in 1978, showed what was missing: the third-rank defence. The authors of the report on Browne's challenge say that players got stuck about fifteen moves from the end, not knowing how to cross the rook's rank, and that the books of the time were no help there. Nunn, who studied the endgame with the tablebases, wrote that a strong player can work out the second rank by calculation, but the third has to be known beforehand. In practice it still decides games. In 1992 Hannes Stefánsson beat Karsten Müller by going through the third rank, the second and Philidor. In 2006, in Pamplona, Morozevich did everything right for dozens of moves against Jakovenko and, with the rook almost won, pressed his pieces against the cornered king: the rook sacrificed itself with check and the game ended in stalemate.
practice: The position from Browne's rematch, the worst there is. With perfect play it takes 31 moves to win the rook, and you have fifty. Bring the king, take the checks away, break the barriers one by one and reach Philidor.
